title: The Chinese and Greek painters
hookLine: one team paints a wall, the other only polishes theirs until it mirrors everything (Masnavi 1.3467ff)
tomorrow: of course there are rude people

cards: Some people fill a room. They've got the stories, the opinions, the funny voices, and they're great company.
And then there's the other kind: the friend you tell something to, and somehow, when they listen, you see your own life more clearly. They don't add much. They reflect.
You leave feeling more like yourself. Both are gifts. But Rumi tells a story about a contest between the two, a painting contest judged by a king.
One team brings a hundred colors. The other brings none at all.

teach.b: It's in Book One of the Masnavi. The Chinese painters say: we're the better artists. The Greeks, by which Rumi means the painters of the Byzantine lands, say: no, we are.
So the king sets a test. Each team gets a room, facing each other, with a curtain hung between.
The Chinese ask the king for a hundred colors, and every morning they collect more paint from his treasury. The Greeks say: no colors are right for our work. All we do is remove the rust.
They shut their door and polish, day after day, until the wall is as clear and bright as the sky. The Chinese finish first, and beat drums for joy. The king comes in and is amazed by their painting.
Then he goes to the Greeks, and they pull back the curtain.
All the Chinese pictures, reflected in that polished wall, shine back even more beautifully than on the wall where they were painted.

Rumi tells us who the Greeks are: the Sufis, he says, who don't rely on study and books and learning, but have polished their hearts clean of greed, envy and malice. A heart polished like that is a mirror.

It can receive every image, without end. Rumi isn't saying here that learning is useless. He's saying the heart's work isn't adding more, it's clearing away, and a clear heart takes in the whole world.

how: Sufi teachers speak of polishing the heart, and some describe dhikr, the remembrance of God, as the polish that clears it.

o: a heart polished clear enough to reflect everything
a picture of vanity and too much self-regard
a magic glass that shows you the future

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: a hundred colors from the treasury
pulled back to reveal the reflection

s: the Greek painters used no colors at all
they said their work was only to remove the rust, and polished.
the Chinese painting outshone everything in the end
reflected in the polished wall, the same pictures looked even more beautiful.
he's saying the heart's work is clearing away, not adding more.

games.q: you're one of the Greek painters. the other team has a hundred colors. what do you ask the king for?
games.why: they asked for no colors at all. they polished their wall until it reflected everything.

practice: Picture a mirror inside you, a little dusty from the week. With each out-breath, imagine one layer of dust coming off: a worry, a grudge, an old comparison.
Don't add anything; just clear, slowly, the way you'd clean a window or a table.

wordCard.voice: Mirror. One team paints with a hundred colors; the other only polishes its wall, until it reflects everything more beautifully, like a heart cleared of greed and envy. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: a mirror. for Rumi, the polished heart.

carryVoice: Your line: polish the mirror. A clear heart takes in everything. Until tomorrow.
